analytic.title: Asynchronous Data Sharing in Multiprocessor Real-Time Systems Using Process Consensus

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: This paper presents an approach to implementing fully asynchronous reader/writer mechanisms which addresses the problems of priority inversion and blocking among tasks within multiprocessor real-time systems. The approach is conceived from the concept of process consensus that the writer and the reader come to an agreement on accessing the shared data before proceeding to carry out their respective data operations. Because neither locking operations nor repeated actions of read-and-check are involved, the shared data can be accessed at any time by the writer and all the readers in a manner not only wait-free but also loopfree. In addition, sharing data via this approach introduces no impact upon either timing behaviour or schedulability of any task in the system. Hence the approach helps to remove priority inversion and blocking incurred by the commonly used lock-based synchronization mechanisms.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The implementation of shared data objects is a very important issue in multiprocessor real-time systems because the commonly used lock-based mutual exclusion mechanism not only reduces parallelism but also introduces priority inversion in which a task has to wait for the lock on a shared data object to be released by another task with lower priority. When data sharing is across processors, a task may also be blocked waiting for tasks running on different processors. Such waiting and blocking cause problems in both the scheduler and the schedulability of the task set.

To avoid waiting and blocking, the 'read-and-check' loop has been introduced to allow concurrent reading while writing [9,11]. The reader, instead of locking the shared data, checks after each read operation for a non-interfered reading and repeats the read-and-check if necessary. Alternatively, the writer is made to write multiple copies of the shared data so that the reader can obtain an uncorrupted version of the shared data [15,20]. These approaches are lock-free or non-blocking because no locking mechanism is involved and the shared data is accessible at any time. However, repeated operations of read-and-check imposes an increase in reader's response time while writing multiple buffer slots increases writer's execution time and space requirement. For real-time applications, lock-free data sharing mechanisms are suitable and beneficial only if the timing behaviour of tasks is still predictable and analyzable.

Simpson presented a four-slot y fully asynchronous data sharing mechanism with which a single writer communicates with a single reader [16]. His approach is loop-free in the sense that no 'read-and-check' loop is used. Other four-slot constructions were presented by Anderson and Gouda [3], and Tromp [18] in their studies on atomic registers. By allocating two buffer slots and two control variables for each additional reader, Simpson's four-slot mechanism can be generalized to the case of multiple readers [17]. For n readers, a buffer of 2n + 2 slots is required. With hardware supported concurrency control operations, the space requirement can be reduced in realizing loop-free asynchronous data sharing. In [4], a three-slot loop-free mechanism is implemented using the Compare-and-Swap instruction. A generalized n + 2 -slot mechanism for n readers is described in [5]. Both mechanisms are developed with the notion of 'helping' in which the writer, after writing a new version of the shared data, helps the reader to determine the buffer slot to read.

In this paper, a consensus-based approach to implementing loop-free asynchronous reader/writer mechanisms in shared-memory multiprocessor real-time systems is prey A slot refers to the storage in data buffer holding a copy of the shared data. Through executing the consensus protocol, the writer and each reader, as a reader-writer pair, come to an agreement on accessing the shared data before proceeding to perform their respective data operations. Thus data objects are shared in a loop-free manner with operations simpler than the Compare-and-Swap instruction while the space overhead is still kept low.

In the remaining of this paper, Section 2 describes the computational model and Section 3 discusses the requirements of asynchronous data sharing within a multiprocessor real-time system. In Section 4, process consensus is briefly described. Loop-free data sharing mechanisms for single reader and multiple readers are developed in Section 5 and Section 6 respectively. Finally, Section 7 concludes this paper.

div.head: The Computational Model
div.p: Although data sharing is common in many different types of applications, addressing the issues within sharedmemory multiprocessor real-time systems is of interest in this work. Figure 1 depicts the architecture of a typical shared-memory multiprocessor system. A set of tasks with timing constraints are running on the system. Each task is sequentially executed on its host processor while there are shared data objects for the purpose of intertask communication. Since allocation of tasks is not addressed here, tasks sharing the same data may be running on different processors. On each processor, tasks are scheduled to run on a priority basis. The writer process and all the reader processes are therefore subjected to preemption, at any time instance during their execution, by tasks with higher priorities. However, the execution of each task must be completed before its associated deadline.

Assuming that all processor-to-memory communication and memory operations follow the sequential consistency principle [2,10,12], the integrity of shared data, when accessed by two or more tasks at the same time, is thus guaranteed at the level of single basic memory unit such as a byte or a word. It is also assumed that machine instructions which enforce atomic read-modify-write operation to a shared memory location are provided. Data sharing mechanisms described in this paper are implemented with the Test-and-Set instruction which, as shown in Figure 2, reads and then writes the designated memory location L in a single atomic memory operation [8]. Note that one memory bit is enough for the operation of Test-and-Set although the data type of integer is used in the figure.

div.head: Asynchronous Data Sharing
div.p: The data sharing problem addressed in this paper concerns a number of reader processes accessing a data object maintained by a single writer process. Since there is no restriction on the size of shared data, neither the read operation nor the write operation is considered to be atomic.
Solutions featuring concurrent reading while writing are the focus here. Essentially, the following requirements must be satisfied [11,15,16]:
Both the integrity and the coherence of data values obtained by the readers must be guaranteed.
The latest complete version of the shared data produced by the writer must always be available for accessing by the readers.
The mechanism must be symmetrical among all the processors within the system. The writer and the readers are not necessarily running on the same processor.
Nothing is assumed about the speed and the duration of either the read operation or the write operation. Neither is any assumption made on the relative speed among tasks in the system.

The implication from the above requirements is that data may be overwritten, if the writer is faster than the readers, or repeatedly read when the readers are faster than the writer. Thus, in the general case, there is no precedence restriction between the writer and any of the readers.

For a real-time application, data sharing mechanisms with the non-blocking property are most desirable. In particular, a mechanism that is free of any 'read-and-check' loop in addition to being lock-free is sought. The loop-free property is justified by observations on the following runtime behaviors: Repeated execution of a 'read-and-check' loop increases both the worst-case execution time of the reader task and the response time of lower priority tasks running on the same processor.
In case the writing operation might be preempted by a reader, all readers with 'read-and-check' loops running on the writer's host processor cannot have priorities higher than the writer.
The readers running on processors other than the writer's host processor may suffer from excessive repeated 'read-and-check' operations when the writer is preempted during its writing operation.

Besides, the 'read-and-check' loop tends to increase the loading on the processor-memory interconnect of the system by repeatedly accessing the shared data thereby imposes negative effect upon system performance.

div.head: The Reader/Writer Consensus
div.p: In the consensus problem, a set of processes must come to an agreement on a common output value; trivial solutions in which processes agree on a predetermined value are not allowed [19]. The decision made on this output value is based on initial states of the processes, not their relative speeds.

Reaching consensus among asynchronous processes has been extensively studied from various aspects [1,7,19]. In particular, Herlihy showed that achieving consensus in shared-memory systems requires synchronization primitives and shared data with the Test-and-Set operation can resolve consensus between two processes [7].

Figure 3 sketches a protocol in which processes P1 and P2 reach consensus on their returned values after executing the Test-and-Set instruction on the control variable L1. It is derived from [7] to demonstrate the construction of a consensus protocol. Following the same approach, a writer and a reader can achieve consensus with the Test-and-Set instruction.

In this paper, the concept of process consensus is applied to help avoid the interference between the reader and the writer so that the integrity of the shared data can be maintained. The main theme is that if the writer knows, by reaching consensus with the reader, which buffer slot the reader is reading or will be reading, then the writer is able to avoid writing into the same buffer slot. A loop-free fully asynchronous data sharing mechanism thus can be achieved.

div.head: A Three-Slot Asynchronous Mechanism
div.p: This section describes a loop-free asynchronous data sharing mechanism based upon the consensus between a single writer and a single reader. No 'read-and-check' loop is involved in reading the shared data and only one copy of the shared data is written by the writer each time during its execution. The mechanism will be called the three-slot asynchronous mechanism or the three-slot mechanism for short because three buffer slots are allocated to accommodate the shared data. Three buffer slots are necessary because while the reader is accessing a buffer slot, at least two buffer slots must be available for the writer to alternately write into. Thus the reader can always obtain the shared data from the buffer slot last completely written while the writer is busy writing a new version of the shared data.

div.head: The Design
div.p: The development of the three-slot asynchronous mechanism involves the design of a protocol which, without employing any data locking operation, coordinates access to the shared data so that the reader and the writer never access the same buffer slot at the same time. Among the three buffer slots, the reader shall read the buffer slot holding the latest version of the shared data and the writer, when delivering a new version of the shared data, must write into a buffer slot other than the one being accessed by the reader. The writer is able to choose a buffer slot safe to write into by reaching consensus with the reader on the buffer slot being accessed and avoiding writing into the same buffer slot.

In other words, the index of the buffer slot being read by the reader is the consensus to be reached between the reader and the writer before carrying out their respective data operations. A consensus protocol is thus of primary importance in the design.

It is observed that each time when an execution instance of the writer starts, a buffer slot other than the last written one must be available to be written. This is not the same for the reader because the same buffer slot can be repeatedly read by consecutive execution instances of the reader before the writer completes writing a new version of the shared data. Therefore the consensus is considered separately from the reader's side and the writer's side in designing the consensus protocol. In the following, the time span, during an execution instance of the reader, from the time the reader prepares to reach consensus with the writer to the time the consensus is reached at the reader's side is referred to as an r-consensus session. The consensus reached by the reader at the end of an r-consensus session is naturally called rconsensus. At the writer's side, the terms w-consensus session and w-consensus assume similar meanings. The buffer slot which is being accessed by the reader is referred to as an engaged slot. A buffer slot that the writer can safely write into without interfering with the reader is called a safe slot.

To indicate the buffer slot keeping the latest version of the shared data, a control variable LATEST is employed to hold the index of that buffer slot. The value of LATEST needs to be updated by the writer after a new version of the shared data is written, and the current value of LATEST is obtained by the reader before accessing a buffer slot. Both the reader and the writer therefore use the value of LATEST, as independently seen from each execution instance, to achieve their respective r-consensus and w-consensus. The r-consensus is used by the reader to access a buffer slot while the wconsensus is used by the writer to locate the engaged slot in order to avoid writing into. This suggests the dominant role of the reader in the consensus protocol. The reader is thus designed to assume the responsibility of resetting the control variable L1 each time it initiates an r-consensus session. At the writer's side, when the writer executes the consensus protocol, it is necessary for the writer to know whether it should achieve a new w-consensus or the previously achieved consensus is to be followed. Two control variables are required for this purpose. The control variable L2 is employed to convey the signal from the reader to the writer that a new consensus is to be achieved while the other control variable PRECON is solely used by the writer to record the newly achieved consensus. The protocol designed to resolve the consensus between a reader and a faster writer is outlined in Figure 4.

This causes no problem if the writer chooses as a safe slot a buffer slot other than the ones indicated by the value of LATEST and the w-consensus.

div.p: Figure 5 shows the three-slot asynchronous mechanism implemented from the design discussed above. Its construction is composed of a three-slot buffer, six control variables, the consensus protocol (shown in Figure 4), the writer process and the reader process.

The essential part of the mechanism is the consensus protocol through which the reader and the writer come to an agreement on the engaged slot. As shown in Figure 4, the values of LATEST, as seen respectively by the reader and the writer, are used in achieving consensus.

div.head: Correctness
div.p: The three-slot asynchronous mechanism must preserve the properties of safety and orderliness to ensure that data sharing is correctly implemented. Its correctness can be proved by showing that all the desired properties are maintained [6]. Due to the limited space here, these properties are stated while the proofs have to be omitted.

div.head: Notations and Terminologies
div.p: The notations R j and W k , where 1 j and 1 k, are used in the following to denote respectively the jth execution instance of the reader task and the kth execution instance of the writer task. Notations c j R and c k W denote respectively the r-consensus achieved during R j and the w-consensus achieved during W k . The value of LATEST obtained by R j is denoted as l j R . Similarly, l k W denotes the value of LATEST as seen by W k before W k updates LATEST.

Without loss of generality, let W 0 be the process which initializes the shared data buffer. A mapping from an execution instance of the reader to that of the writer can be defined: for each execution instance of the reader, R j , there is an execution instance of the writer, denoted as !R j , that writes the version of the shared data obtained by R j .

To express the temporal precedence relation among execution of operations, two symbols, namely and k, are used. The symbol assumes the same meaning as that of the symbol ! used in Lamport's model of system execution [13]. If the execution of P 1 op i , an operation car- ried out by process P 1 , can be asserted to complete before the execution of another operation P 2 op j starts, then the temporal precedence relation between these two operations is expressed as P 1 op i P 2 op j . When the execution of P 1 is completed before the start of P 2 , it is expressed as P 1 P 2 . The symbol k is used to denote the execution overlap between concurrently executed operations or processes. The expression P 1 op i k P 2 op j denotes that the execution of P 1 op i overlaps that of P 2 op j . Assume similar meaning for the expression of the form P 1 k P 2 . The expression P 1 6 P 2 means that either P 2 P 1 or P 1 k P 2 holds.

div.head: The Safety Property
div.p: It is required that, for the three-slot asynchronous mechanism to hold the safety property, both the reader and the writer are free of interference from each other. Clearly, this property holds if the execution of the writer does not overlap the execution of the reader. When running in a fully asynchronous manner, the mechanism must ensure that the reader and the writer never access the same buffer slot if their respective data operations overlap.

Based on all the above properties, it is seen that the three-slot asynchronous mechanism correctly implements the data object shared between a single writer and a single reader. Moreover, by inspection, it uses the minimum buffer slot count of three with no 'read-and-check' loop.

div.head: The n-Reader Asynchronous Mechanism
div.p: The three-slot asynchronous mechanism described in last section can be generalized to the case of multiple readers. In this section, a loop-free asynchronous data sharing mechanism for one writer and n readers is developed from the three-slot mechanism. The names n-reader asynchronous mechanism and multi-reader mechanism are used interchangeably when referring to this mechanism.

div.head: The Design
div.p: The main idea in designing the n-reader asynchronous mechanism is to consider sharing data between a single writer and multiple readers as the combination of multiple instances of the data sharing problem between a single writer and a single reader. In other words, the single writer is paired with each of the n readers so that the three-slot mechanism can be adapted to implement the shared data for each reader-writer pair. This comes from the observation that there should be neither dependency nor mutual interference among the readers and all the readers are running independently as well as concurrently. Therefore symmetry exists among the readers and the interactions between the writer and any of the readers are the same. However, it is not meant by this idea to simply make n replicas of the three-slot mechanism for the n reader-writer pairs because doing so results in unnecessary overhead on both space and timing -3n buffer slots and, during every execution of the writer, writing n copies of the shared data.

In allocating multiple buffer slots to hold the shared data, the multi-reader mechanism is aimed at consuming the space within shared memory as little as possible. Since two buffer slots are needed to be alternately written when a reader is busy accessing a buffer slot, the number of required buffer slots should be n + 2 which is two more than the maximum number of the buffer slots being accessed by the readers at a time. Note that three buffer slots are allocated when there is only one reader.

To coordinate accessing the buffer slots, the consensus protocol shown in Figure 4 can be adapted to each readerwriter pair. Since the protocol is only capable of resolving consensus between two processes [7], each reader-writer pair requires its own set of control variables except LATEST. There is no need for multiple copies of LATEST because the readers maintain their own copies of its value.

Based upon the above discussion, all the n readers have the same operations as the reader in the three-slot mechanism. At the other side, the writer has to individually resolve its w-consensus with every reader in order to locate all the engaged slots. To allocate a safe slot to deliver new version of the shared data, the writer can choose among the n + 2 buffer slots any one with its index value different from the values of LATEST and those w-consensuses.

div.head: The Implementation
div.p: The completed design of the n-reader asynchronous mechanism is implemented as shown in Figure 6. Its construction consists of a n + 2 slot buffer, 5n + 1 control variables, the consensus protocol, a procedure to allocate a safe slot, the reader processes numbered from 1 to n and the writer process.

The function GetSlot is the crux of this mechanism. It assumes the responsibility of allocating a safe slot for the writer to deliver new version of the shared data. A local array of n+ 2 components, namely InUse, is used to indicate the status whether a buffer slot is engaged. GetSlot carries out its function in three steps. Firstly, as shown by line g.1, all the components of InUse are initialized to f a l s e assum-g g g ing no buffer slot is being read. During the second step, the consensus protocol is executed against each reader to locate the buffer slot engaged to that reader. Each engaged slot is marked by setting the corresponding component of InUse to true (line g.2 to g.4). Since a reader may initiate a new consensus session and accesses another buffer slot while GetSlot is holding previous consensus, the buffer slot indicated by LATEST is marked at the end of this step (line g.5). This is because all such readers will be accessing the buffer slot indexed by the value held in LATEST. At its last step (line g.6), InUse is searched to find an unmarked buffer slot. The first unmarked buffer slot is selected as the safe slot and its index is returned to the writer.

div.head: Correctness
div.p: Because of the symmetry among the reader-writer pairs, the properties of the three-slot asynchronous mechanism are preserved, between the writer and each of the readers, by the n-reader asynchronous mechanism. In the following, the notation R i (1 i n) stands for an arbitrary one among the n readers.

From the construction shown in Figure 6, it can be seen that its safety property relies the function GetSlot to successfully choose a safe slot for the writer to write into. This is asserted by the following theorem. Theorem 6.1 The function GetSlot in the n-reader asynchronous mechanism returns the index value of a buffer slot that is safe for the writer to write into. Following Theorem 6.1, the safety property of the nreader asynchronous mechanism can be asserted.

div.head: Property 6.2
div.p: The n-reader asynchronous mechanism maintains the safety property.

As with the three-slot mechanism, the multi-reader mechanism must maintain the orderliness property. Property 5.5 holds individually for each reader. With multiple readers, it is necessary that the criterion C3 is generalized to:
C4. If R j a R j 0 b holds, then !R j 0 b 6 !R j a where R j a and R j 0 b are not necessarily execution instances of the same reader.

div.head: Property 6.3
div.p: In the n-reader asynchronous mechanism, criterion C4 is satisfied.
All the above proves the correctness of the n-reader asynchronous mechanism.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: This paper has shown that loop-free asynchronous data sharing mechanisms can be realized with process consensus. The approach is demonstrated by developing a consensus protocol for a reader and a writer using the atomic Test-and-Set operation. Data sharing mechanisms using this protocol are efficient in both space and time in the sense that only n + 2 buffer slots are required for n readers and the writer only writes a single copy of the shared data. The functionality of these mechanisms is independent of task allocation and there is no increase of response time, due to blocking or repeated operations, imposed upon any task in the system. When used in a real-time application, both the timing behaviour and the schedulability of tasks are not affected in any form. This approach therefore helps to remove priority inversion and blocking incurred by the commonly used lock-based synchronization mechanisms.

Although this consensus-based approach is aimed at addressing those issues arisen from sharing data among tasks within multiprocessor real-time systems, it is as well suited to general multiprocessor applications. In addition, there would be no difficulty to achieve implementations using other memory read-modify-write instructions such as Fetch-and-Add or Exchange (swapping data values held by a register and a memory location) instruction.
